title: Estimating Average and Local Average Treatment Effects of Education When Compulsory Schooling Laws Really Matter
research_question: What are the earnings returns to an additional year of schooling for individuals induced to stay in school by minimum school-leaving-age requirements? Specifically, how do average returns for a broadly affected population compare to returns for the smaller subpopulation affected by similar policy shifts in other countries?
data_description: The analysis uses microdata from the British and Northern Irish General Household Surveys (GHHS). The baseline sample covers survey years 1984 through 1998, with alternative specifications extending the surveys to 2006 (and one specification beginning in 1979). The unit of observation is an individual respondent, restricted to those born between 1921 and 1951 and aged 28 to 64 (with one alternative restricting to ages 28–60, and another dropping individuals who left full-time schooling after age 18). Key variables include age finished full-time education and log annual earnings. Sample sizes range from roughly 8,000 (Northern Ireland) to over 80,000 (combined Great Britain and Northern Ireland). Data are aggregated into birth-cohort/region cell means and weighted by cell size; observations are clustered by birth cohort and region (Great Britain or Northern Ireland). The 1994 British earnings measure, accidentally omitted in earlier work, is included.
institutional_context: The setting is the United Kingdom's mid-twentieth-century reforms that raised the minimum school-leaving age from 14 to 15. This change took effect in Great Britain in 1947 and in Northern Ireland a decade later, in 1957. Because the prior leaving age of 14 was binding for a large share of youth, the reforms compelled an unusually large fraction—estimated at roughly 40 to 50 percent—of the affected birth cohorts to remain in school for at least one additional year. This stands in contrast to comparable compulsory-schooling reforms in the United States and Canada, which directly affected only a small minority of cohorts. The sharp, cohort-specific timing of the British and Northern Irish reforms, combined with the magnitude of the affected population, provides a setting in which to measure earnings consequences of additional schooling for a broad population rather than a narrow margin of compliers, and permits comparisons of estimates across the two UK regions whose reforms occurred a decade apart.
ground_truth_notes: The confidence is less than 1.0 due to wide confidence intervals and the need for robustness checks.
